title: What it means to be a reading teacher
author: Amy Coombe
summary: Amy Coombe reflects on what it truly means to be a reading teacher — not a label that arrives with a teaching credential but a professional identity constructed through rigorous learning, community, and sustained commitment to the science of reading. Drawing on her experience with Corrective Reading in secondary schools, she shows that most teachers are never trained to teach reading explicitly, yet are expected to do so. The article traces the emotional and professional transformation that comes from building a community of reading teachers who observe each other, share language, and solve problems collectively. Coombe argues that schools systematically underinvest in reading teacher identity and that the consequences fall hardest on struggling readers. She makes the case that becoming a reading teacher — rather than simply a teacher who uses reading — requires a shift in professional self-concept that institutions rarely support. The essay concludes with a call for structural investment in reading teacher formation rather than one-off professional development events.
points: Schools assume reading ability is a given and so never build the infrastructure to train teachers to teach it explicitly.
Building a community of reading teachers creates shared language and mutual observation that changes individual classroom practice.
Secondary schools carry the accumulated weight of years of reading instruction that never happened — and struggling students pay the price.
Being a reading teacher is a professional identity, not just a skill — and identities require cultivation, community, and sustained institutional investment.
Corrective Reading works because it makes teacher learning visible and gives teachers a framework they can observe, iterate on, and share.
